title: Organisms and their Environment
seo_title: Secondary 4 Biology: Organisms and their Environment Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_code: O-Level Biology (6093): Organisms and their Environment
standard_text: Define ecological terms such as habitat, population, community, ecosystem, producer, consumer, decomposer and trophic level; describe food chains and food webs and the flow of energy through them; explain energy losses between trophic levels; interpret pyramids of numbers and biomass; describe the carbon cycle; describe the effects of human activities such as deforestation, water pollution and eutrophication, and the need for conservation (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 4 O-Level Biology worksheets on organisms and their environment: food chains and webs, energy flow, pyramids, the carbon cycle, eutrophication, deforestation and conservation in Singapore. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Only about 10% of the energy passes to the next trophic level.
body_html:
How to think about it

Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

  • Producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer; arrows show energy flow.
  • At each level energy is lost in respiration (heat), faeces and uneaten parts, so pyramids get narrower.
  • Carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, decay and combustion return it.
  • Human impact: deforestation, eutrophication, overfishing. Conservation: reserves, quotas, seed banks.
Example

Producers 20 000 kJ, consumers 2000 kJ. Efficiency?

2000 ÷ 20 000 × 100

Answer: 10%

Example

Fertiliser in a lake → ?

algal bloom

decomposers use oxygen

Answer: fish die

Common mistakes

  • Saying energy is recycled.
  • Drawing arrows to the food that is eaten.
  • Saying a pyramid of numbers is always upright.
  • Saying eutrophication is caused by too few nutrients.

faq.q: Why is energy lost between trophic levels?
faq.a: Organisms use energy for respiration and lose it as heat; some is lost in faeces and urine, and some parts are not eaten.
Extra nutrients such as nitrates enter water and cause an algal bloom. Plants below die, decomposers use up the oxygen and fish die.
Plants take in carbon dioxide in photosynthesis. Carbon passes along food chains and returns to the air by respiration, decomposition and combustion.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the squid eats small fish. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Which term means all the populations of different species living in an area?
items.e: A community: all the populations of different species living in an area.

items.q: Look at the food web of a pond. In this web, the frog eats dragonfly nymphs and snails. What kind of consumer is it?

items.q: Which term means a group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time?
items.e: A population: a group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time.

items.q: Why is it more efficient for humans to eat plants than animals that eat plants?
c: Less energy is lost because there is one fewer trophic level.
items.e: More people can be fed from the same land.

items.q: What is a producer?

an organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis
items.e: A producer: an organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the sea urchin eats seaweed. What kind of consumer is it?

items.q: What is an ecosystem?

items.q: In eutrophication, which step comes straight after this: “Light cannot reach plants below the surface, so they die.”

Decomposers break down dead plants and algae and use up oxygen.
Fish and other animals die from lack of oxygen.
Fertiliser containing nitrates and phosphates enters the lake.
items.e: Nutrients → algal bloom → plants die → decomposers use oxygen → fish die.
